title: The Art of Value Investing | John Heins & Whitney Tilson | Talks at Google
description:
“John Heins and Whitney Tilson, co-founders of the Value Investor Insight newsletter, have done a thorough job of explaining how to look for stocks that are trading at significant discounts to what they are worth — the concept known as the value style of investing.…the authors present a clear framework for ferreting out undervalued companies.”
—The New York Times

About the book:
In The Art of Value Investing, John Heins and Whitney Tilson offer a comprehensive set of answers to the questions that everyone investing seriously in the stock market should have thought through clearly before committing his or her hard-earned capital to the endeavor. What market efficiencies will I try to exploit? What analytical edge can I hope to have? How specifically will I decide to buy or sell? For answers, they call on market-beating money managers – including such investing luminaries as Seth Klarman, David Einhorn, Bill Ackman, Howard Marks, Mason Hawkins and Julian Robertson – who have graced the pages over the past ten years of their highly regarded newsletter, Value Investor Insight. To illustrate one of the equity investor’s most important tasks – how to value a company – they will present a particularly relevant current case study … on Google.
 
About the authors:
John Heins is the co-founder and President of Value Investor Media, Inc. and Editor-in-Chief of Value Investor Insight and SuperInvestor Insight. Previously, he served as CEO of Bertelsmann AG’s U.S. magazine subsidiary, ran AOL’s Personal Finance business and was a reporter and staff writer for Forbes magazine. He holds a bachelor’s degree in Economics from the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School and earned an M.B.A. from Stanford University.

summary: The speakers argue that Google represents a rare opportunity for a large company to sustain high growth rates, noting that its core business is highly profitable and that the stock price may not fully reflect the value of expensed investments in future options like self-driving cars. While acknowledging past mistakes in shorting companies like Tesla and Netflix, the speakers maintain a bullish view on Google's potential, contrasting it with Salesforce.com, which they believe has extremely low odds of replicating Google's success over the next decade. The discussion also highlights Amazon's strategy of reinvesting profits for growth and Facebook's dominant business model, but focuses primarily on the valuation and growth prospects of Google.

claims.claim: The speaker believes Google's core business is highly profitable and that the stock is not as expensive as it appears due to expensed investments in future options like self-driving cars.
claims.quote: And I might give Google credit for that and say, how much is their core business really earning, x-ing out all these expenses. And it might be quite a bit of expenses, and you might actually say Google's core business trading for 15 times earnings or something like a market multiple
claims.speaker: Whitney Tilson

claims.claim: The speaker expects Google to continue growing revenues at 20% annually, which would double earnings in four years, making the stock a potential double.
claims.quote: You continue to grow your revenues 20% for the next four years, if your margins just stay flat, that means the earnings go up 20% a year. That's a double in four years. A 20 multiple or so, if you can continue to grow at 20% is a reasonable thing to assume.
claims.speaker: Whitney Tilson

claims.claim: The speaker states he would not bet against Google and is intrigued by the company, noting it is a rare large company capable of such high growth rates.
claims.quote: So I certainly wouldn't bet against it. The question is is for a guy who only owns 15 stocks, is this one of the best 15 stocks in the universe I can find? That's the real question.
claims.speaker: Whitney Tilson

claims.claim: The speaker believes the odds of Salesforce.com looking like Google over the next 10 years are extremely low, citing that 99 out of 100 companies at such extreme valuations turn out to be lousy investments.
claims.quote: And so investors are sort of betting that that's going to look like Google over the next 10 years or so, and I think the odds of that are extremely low. In general, you guys are the outlier. As a general rule, 99 out of 100 companies that grade at such extreme valuations turn out to be lousy, if not catastrophic investments.
claims.speaker: Whitney Tilson

claims.claim: The speaker admits to making a mistake by holding Google stock for years while believing it was doomed.
claims.quote: I'll admit, when he's talking about his stupid mistake with Google, I had Apple stock. And my son, who is now 22 years old, when he was born. I put it in his college savings fund. And I had Apple stock that did nothing for years.
claims.speaker: John Heins

claims.claim: The speaker admits to shorting Tesla but later gained appreciation for it and thinks it is an incredible company.
claims.quote: Well, compare that to a Tesla, which is I was stupid enough to short, and then gained appreciation for it and think it's an incredible company. But you see, they actually have to make stuff, and then they have to ship it, and they have inventory, et cetera, et cetera.
claims.speaker: Whitney Tilson

claims.claim: The speaker believes Facebook has the second or greatest business model in the world due to its winner-take-all nature and zero incremental cost to add members.
claims.quote: And Facebook got killed post IPO and it went from 50 or something, down to 20 or something. You guys actually might have been able to figure that out, whereas I wasn't. Because I'm not out here. I don't know the people at all. But Facebook, I think you guys have the second best business model in the world. I actually think Facebook may well have the greatest business model in the world.
claims.speaker: Whitney Tilson

claims.claim: The speaker mentions buying Astroturf.com when it comes public as a potential mistake to avoid, implying caution for new public offerings.
claims.quote: So I'm going to go buy Astroturf.com when it comes public, or do something stupid, right? So you just have to be patient. And be content. We're in sort of a low return world, so hang out, live beneath your means, save money, and wait for better opportunities.
claims.speaker: Whitney Tilson

claims.claim: The speaker notes that the crowd was right on Google and that the stock was an 11-bagger, implying it was undervalued.
claims.quote: The crowd was right on Google. If anything, the crowd didn't appreciate Google enough. We now know, stock was an 11-bagger.
claims.speaker: WHITNEY TILSON

claims.claim: The speaker admits Netflix was a massively better company than he thought and that his short thesis pillars were wrong.
claims.quote: Netflix was a massively better company than I thought. And the key pillars of my short thesis were there's no moat around the business, and sort of wacky management, and competitors are going to come in and eat their lunch. All of my pillars of my short thesis were wrong.
claims.speaker: WHITNEY TILSON

claims.claim: The speaker believes Netflix could become a world-beater after they made a bold bet to invest in streaming content and forgo current profitability, similar to Amazon's strategy.
claims.quote: Netflix, they were selling an earnings growth story, and then they decided the hell with earnings growth, hell with earnings at all. We're just going to invest in the future. We're become like Amazon. And all the investors that were in there for the earnings interest story sold the stock. But I was like, you know what, I think this company could be a world beater someday.
claims.speaker: WHITNEY TILSON

claims.claim: The speaker notes that Amazon has never made a profit because of its policy of plowing every penny of profit back into future growth, and the market has not destroyed its stock.
claims.quote: Amazon's been doing that for 20 years. They've never made a profit because they have a policy of taking every single penny of profit and plowing it back in to future growth. And you know what, the market hasn't destroyed Amazon stock.
claims.speaker: WHITNEY TILSON

claims.claim: The speaker suggests that while Google is a great company, the stock price may not be a value because the market is overly enamored with its future, making it a poor investment.
claims.quote: OK, Google is a great company, but that doesn't always mean that investing in Google stock is a great investment. It may be that the market is so enamored with Google's future that the price you'd have to pay it own a share of Google isn't a value, and it won't be a great investment.
claims.speaker: JOHN HEINS
